items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 2 so that it gives college admissions readers, who look for personal reflection, a clear sense of what the pool came to mean to her. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Over those summers, I came to see the pool as one of the few places in town where strangers become neighbors.
options.label: correct
options.why: Offers a personal insight drawn from her experience and previews the essay's claim, which is what admissions readers look for.

options.text: Public pools across the country offer recreation, safety training, and relief from summer heat.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes a general statement about pools nationwide and leaves out the writer's own reflection.

options.text: Lifeguards must be certified in first aid and must renew that certification every two years.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a procedural fact that has nothing to do with the essay's reflective claim.

options.text: Honestly, the pool is basically the best spot in Calder Falls, and everybody knows it.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Uses casual, boastful phrasing and an unsupported claim instead of thoughtful reflection.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that explains how the council's decision weakens the role she says the pool plays in the community. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Without those hours, the families who most needed a shared place to meet their neighbors were the ones left out.
options.label: correct
options.why: Links the lost evening hours to the claim that the pool brings strangers together, showing who is now cut off.

options.text: The evening lifeguards were reassigned to the morning shift, which was already fully staffed.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a staffing detail that has no basis in the draft and does not explain the effect on the community.

options.text: The council also discussed repaving Delmont Avenue and repainting the library that night.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Moves to unrelated agenda items rather than commenting on the pool decision.

options.text: Even so, the pool stayed open, so the petition clearly achieved everything it set out to do.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Says the outcome was a full success, which goes against the writer's point that the cut did real harm.

items.stem: In sentence 3, the writer wants to keep her affectionate, gently amused tone toward Mr. Okafor. Which choice for the underlined portion, "tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself," best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: (as it is now) tells me the water temperature as if I had not measured it myself
options.label: correct
options.why: The mild exaggeration shows fondness and light humor without any mockery.

options.text: annoyingly lectures me about the water temperature like I am clueless
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Sounds irritated and dismissive, not affectionate.

options.text: reports the water temperature, which is recorded hourly on a clipboard
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Drops the humor and turns the moment into a flat procedural note.

options.text: rudely corrects my measurements of the water temperature every morning
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: "Rudely" adds hostility, which works against the warm portrait.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 12 so that it is concise and states her lesson without repetition. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public only if its users show up and speak up where decisions are made.
options.label: correct
options.why: Removes the repeated "I learned" and the wordy phrasing but keeps the full lesson.

options.text: What I learned is that the lesson I learned is that public spaces need people to speak up for them.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Shortens the sentence but keeps the redundant "learned" construction.

options.text: I learned that public spaces matter to everyone in many different ways.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Concise, but it loses the specific point about showing up where decisions are made.

options.text: I learned that a public space stays public, so its users show up wherever decisions are made.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "So" reverses the condition and makes it sound as if staying public causes people to show up.

items.stem: In sentence 10, the writer wants to join the two independent clauses correctly while keeping the contrast between them. Which choice for the underlined portion, "open, but it cut," best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: open, but it cut
options.label: correct
options.why: A comma before the coordinating conjunction "but" correctly joins the two independent clauses and shows contrast.

options.text: open, it cut
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Creates a comma splice between two independent clauses.

options.text: open but, it cut
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Puts the comma after the conjunction, which is the wrong place.

options.text: open, so it cut
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "So" signals cause and effect, but the sentence calls for a contrast.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that gives evidence for the specific claim that students without transfer agreements can lose time retaking courses they already passed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Before Calloway Valley signed its agreement with Ridgeline, one Harlan Ferry student told our staff she had repeated three passed courses, costing her a full extra semester.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a concrete case of passed courses being retaken and time being lost, which is exactly what sentence 11 claims.

options.text: Tuition at Calloway Valley costs much less per credit than at either state university, which lets many patrons save money for the later years of a degree.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Supports the point about low cost in sentence 9, not the claim about lost semesters without agreements.

options.text: The advisors who come to Transfer Night are patient and friendly, and several of them started their own degrees at a community college years ago.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Describes the event's advisors. It gives no evidence that missing agreements make students repeat courses.

options.text: Every college in the state, without exception, now accepts every course from every other college, so no student will ever repeat a class again.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: An unsupported overstatement that also contradicts sentence 11 instead of supporting it.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that admits transfer agreements have limits while still arguing that readers should come to Transfer Night. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Not every course or major is covered by such an agreement, which is exactly why a conversation with an advisor before enrolling is worth an evening.
options.label: correct
options.why: Admits a real limit, then uses that limit as a reason to attend, so the qualification still serves the post's claim.

options.text: Agreements like that one guarantee that every class a student takes will count toward any degree at any university the student chooses.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Overstates the claim even more instead of qualifying it.

options.text: Because so many courses fall outside these agreements, most returning students would probably be better off skipping community college entirely.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions a limit but ends up undercutting the post's argument instead of keeping it.

options.text: The library's meeting room was also recently repainted, and new chairs replaced several of the dented folding ones from earlier years.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Off-topic detail that qualifies nothing about transfer pathways.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with an invitation that sounds warm and reassuring to adults who may feel unsure about returning to school, while staying appropriate for a public library blog. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: We hope you will join us; no question is too basic, and no appointment is needed.
options.label: correct
options.why: Warm and welcoming, it addresses uncertain readers' worries, and its register suits a library blog.

options.text: Attendance is recommended for all eligible parties seeking credit evaluation services.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Cold and bureaucratic, which would put off hesitant readers.

options.text: Seriously, just show up already, you have no excuse to keep putting this off.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Pushy and too casual. Its scolding could make unsure adults feel judged. It is also a comma splice.

options.text: If you are finally ready to fix the mistakes you made back in school, come.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Condescending, since it frames readers' pasts as mistakes. That works against the post's second-chance message.

items.stem: In sentence 3, the writer wants to punctuate the phrase that gives the event's date so that it is correctly set off as a nonessential element. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors
options.label: correct
options.why: Commas set off the whole nonessential phrase, and the comma between the day and the date is correct.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The opening comma is missing, so a comma ends up between the subject and the verb.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday April 17 brings advisors
options.label: convention_error
options.why: The closing comma and the comma between the day and the date are both missing, so the phrase is never closed off.

options.text: Our annual Transfer Night; held this year on Thursday, April 17; brings advisors
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Semicolons cannot set off a phrase inside a single clause.

items.stem: Taken as a whole, the passage is best understood as a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: A fifth anniversary of the swap that coincides with a pending school board decision about the library budget
options.label: correct
options.why: The opening fixes the time as 'five Octobers ago,' and the closing paragraphs refer to the board restoring the budget 'tomorrow,' the budget that 'may come back,' and 'whichever way the vote goes,' signalling an upcoming vote.

options.text: A sudden shortage of donated books that threatens to end the monthly swap within the coming year
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage mentions that a bad month yields forty books, but nothing suggests the swap is in danger of ending; the writer expects the habit to outlast the vote.

options.text: A proposal by the art teacher to take over the swap and convert its damaged books into classroom projects
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The art teacher appears only as the recipient of books 'beyond saving'; no proposal to take over the swap is described.

options.text: A decision by the district to restore the librarian to full time while keeping the purchasing allowance reduced
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage states that Mrs. Avendale still works 'two days a week'; no restoration of her hours has occurred, and the budget remains undecided.

items.stem: The writer's references to the school board in paragraphs 4 and 6 suggest that the intended audience most likely consists of

options.text: members of the local community who may influence or follow a decision about school funding
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer warns that 'anyone who tells the school board otherwise is handing them an excuse' and ends with 'whichever way the vote goes,' assuming readers who care about and can speak to the board's decision.

options.text: middle school students who are deciding whether to contribute books to the monthly swap
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Children are described in the third person throughout ('the children who help me,' 'a boy'); the board warnings and budget argument are not aimed at students.

options.text: professional librarians seeking a model for running a swap in other districts
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer insists the swap is 'not a library' and offers no instructions for replicating it; the essay is reflective, not a procedural guide for professionals.

options.text: the school board members themselves, who are being asked directly to vote for restoration
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer does want the budget restored, but the board is referred to as 'them' and 'the board,' never addressed directly, so the audience is those around the board rather than the board itself.

items.stem: The primary purpose of paragraph 3 is to

options.text: explain how the ongoing handling of books distinguishes the swap from passive donation and supports calling it a craft
options.label: correct
options.why: The paragraph opens by asking what a swap does that 'a shelf of donations in the front office does not,' answers 'in the handling,' and closes by saying the slowness is the point because 'a craft is a thing you learn by doing it badly for a long time.'

options.text: demonstrate that the ledger provides more reliable data than the district's own surveys of student reading
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The ledger is one of several tasks described, and the comparison to 'any survey' is a passing remark, not the paragraph's organizing purpose.

options.text: argue that mending damaged books is more valuable to students than purchasing new hardcovers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never ranks mending above buying new books; paragraph 4 explicitly says the swap 'cannot buy the new book everyone is talking about.'

options.text: show that the slow pace of the swap is a weakness the writer has learned to tolerate over five years
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer says 'That slowness is the point,' treating it as the source of the craft's lessons rather than a weakness to be tolerated.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the overarching thesis of the passage?

options.text: The swap is neither charity nor a replacement for the library but a craft whose slow practice teaches children to pass books along
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 frames the swap as 'less a charity than a craft,' paragraph 4 insists it 'is not a library,' and paragraph 6 affirms that the habit of passing books along 'will outlast whichever way the vote goes.'

options.text: The swap has quietly compensated for the budget cut so effectively that the library's reduced funding no longer harms students
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies this, listing what the swap 'cannot do' and warning that such claims hand the board 'an excuse.'

options.text: The school board must restore the library's purchasing allowance before the swap can accomplish anything lasting
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The writer hopes the budget comes back, but the final sentence says the habit will outlast the vote regardless, so the swap's lasting effect does not depend on restoration.

options.text: Children in a small town will reliably share books if an adult keeps careful records of what they borrow
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The ledger is one tool of the craft, and nothing in the passage attributes the children's giving to the record keeping itself.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the sentence "A thousand dollars buys perhaps sixty new hardcovers, in a building with four hundred and ten students" primarily functions as evidence for which of the following claims?

options.text: The library's collection stopped keeping pace with the needs of its readers after the budget was cut
options.label: correct
options.why: The figure sets the scale of the shortfall and is immediately followed by the claim that the shelves 'simply stopped growing' and that new titles appeared in conversations 'but not in the catalog.'

options.text: The librarian's reduction to two days a week was the most damaging part of the district's decision
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence concerns the purchasing allowance, not staffing hours, and the passage never ranks the two losses against each other.

options.text: Secondhand paperbacks can serve students nearly as well as newly purchased hardcovers
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage makes no comparison of the value of secondhand and new books here; paragraph 4 concedes the swap cannot supply new titles at all.

options.text: The children were willing to contribute more books than they took from the first swap
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: That observation belongs to paragraph 1 and concerns the swap, not the library's purchasing power; the budget figure has no bearing on it.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the sentence "I would rather the board restore the budget tomorrow and put me out of business" relates to the sentence immediately before it by

options.text: showing that the writer accepts the consequence of his own warning and does not want the swap used as the excuse he just described
options.label: correct
options.why: Having said that calling the swap a library hands the board 'an excuse,' the writer removes himself from suspicion by preferring restoration even at the cost of the swap's existence.

options.text: conceding that the swap has failed in its original aim and should be replaced by professional staff
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer does not say the swap has failed; paragraphs 5 and 6 go on to argue for its distinctive value and lasting habit.

options.text: shifting the argument away from the swap's limits toward a prediction that the board will act soon
options.label: unsupported
options.why: 'Tomorrow' expresses a wish, not a forecast; paragraph 6 says only that the budget 'may come back.'

options.text: offering a contrasting view that the swap's limits matter less than the writer had previously admitted
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The sentence reinforces rather than contradicts the concession; it takes the limits seriously enough to prefer the swap's own disappearance.

items.stem: In paragraph 2, the comparison of the library's shelves to "a town [that] stops growing when the last factory closes and nobody notices until the graduating class is half its old size" primarily conveys

options.text: a sense that the loss was gradual and easy to overlook until its effects had accumulated
options.label: correct
options.why: The simile follows 'The shelves did not empty overnight' and stresses that 'nobody notices' until a later, visible sign, matching the idea of a slow, unremarked decline.

options.text: an accusation that the district deliberately concealed the effects of the cut from families
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The simile describes an unnoticed decline, not concealment; the writer says 'nobody notices,' assigning no deceit to the district.

options.text: a suggestion that the town's economy, not the school budget, is the real cause of the library's decline
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The factory town is a figure of comparison, not a literal claim about Corbett Hollow's economy; the stated cause is the district trimming its budget.

options.text: a warning that student enrollment will soon fall sharply as a result of the shrinking catalog
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The shrinking graduating class belongs to the comparison's image; the passage draws no causal link from the catalog to enrollment.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the colon in the sentence beginning "There is one thing the swap does that the library, even in its funded years, never quite did" primarily serves to

options.text: withhold the distinctive benefit until the end of the sentence so that it lands with emphasis after the buildup
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon announces that 'one thing' exists without naming it; the colon then delivers 'it makes children into givers of books,' making the claim the focal point.

options.text: introduce a list of several activities that the swap performs more efficiently than the library
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Only a single idea follows the colon, and the writer stresses 'one thing,' not several; nor does the passage claim the swap is more efficient.

options.text: signal a shift from the writer's own voice to the reported words of the children at the table
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: No quotation follows the colon; the writer continues in his own voice to state a claim.

options.text: separate two independent observations that the writer considers equally important
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The second part explains and completes the first rather than standing as a separate, parallel observation.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's description of the swap as "two tables and a notebook and a roll of linen tape" is most effective in advancing the argument because it

options.text: makes the modest inventory concrete so that the claim about seriousness that follows cannot be dismissed as exaggeration
options.label: correct
options.why: The plain list follows 'I do not want to make the swap sound larger than it is' and sets up the 'But' sentence that a craft 'does not have to be large to be serious,' so the understatement earns the assertion.

options.text: reminds readers of the first swap in paragraph 1 in order to show how much the project has expanded since then
options.label: reversal
options.why: The list emphasizes that the swap remains small, the opposite of expansion; the writer is deliberately shrinking, not enlarging, its scale.

options.text: catalogs the supplies the board would need to fund if it chose to adopt the swap in place of the library
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer has already rejected the swap as a replacement, and nothing suggests the board is being asked to fund it.

options.text: conveys the writer's frustration that the project has never received the equipment it deserves
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone is measured and content, not frustrated; the writer treats the small scale as compatible with seriousness rather than as a grievance.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that ends the flyer by reminding garden members that the proposal fits values they already hold as growers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: This garden has always shared its extra seedlings and spare tools with neighbors, and a table and a stronger signal would just be one more thing we share.
options.label: correct
options.why: Ties the proposal to the members' existing habit of sharing, so the ending appeals to values they already hold.

options.text: High-speed internet is now a basic need across the country, and every rural community will have to deal with the gap sooner or later.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves away from this garden and its members' values to a general national claim.

options.text: If the vote fails, students will keep failing quizzes like Caleb did, and the committee will have to explain why it let that happen.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Ends on a threat that blames the readers instead of appealing to their values.

options.text: The signal booster from the co-op in Pell can be installed in about an afternoon by any member who owns a sturdy ladder.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Gives a practical detail rather than a closing appeal to shared values.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that makes an arguable claim and previews both the proposal and the response to members' concerns. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: For about 140 dollars and a picnic table, the garden could give ridge students a warm, connected place to study without harming a single plot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Makes an arguable claim, previews the booster and the table, and answers the worry about the plots.

options.text: Many families on Marrow Ridge still have no internet service at home, which makes school harder for their children this fall.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: States a situation, not an arguable claim, and previews no proposal; the passage also never shows that many families lack service.

options.text: The garden should buy a signal booster for the shed roof so that its Wi-Fi reaches farther into the gravel lot.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Previews only the booster and leaves out the study table and the concerns about the plots.

options.text: Rural internet access is one of the most important problems facing students, parents, and teachers in the county.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Too general; it does not name the garden's proposal at all.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that explains how Caleb's experience supports the claim that students need a reliable connection. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: He knew the material, but a weak signal kept him from practicing it, so the connection decided his grade more than his effort did.
options.label: correct
options.why: Explains how the anecdote shows that unreliable access, not ability, hurt his grade.

options.text: Caleb is a junior this year and hopes to study nursing at a college somewhere in the state after he graduates.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds background about Caleb that has nothing to do with the claim.

options.text: Chemistry is widely considered one of the hardest subjects in high school, especially for students who struggle with math.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Suggests the subject was the problem, which works against the point about the connection.

options.text: His mother has since switched to a different phone plan, though the hotspot still drops out when it rains on the ridge.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Mentions the connection again but does not explain how the example supports the claim.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 10 and 11 concisely, keeping the idea that the table would need no change to the garden's hours. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would give students a place besides a cold car and would need no new hours, since the garden already stays open until dusk.
options.label: correct
options.why: Concise and clear, and it keeps the causal link between the existing hours and needing no new ones.

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car, the garden already stays open until dusk, so no new hours.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Comma splice, and the last clause is a fragment.

options.text: A picnic table under the shed awning, with one outdoor outlet, would let students work somewhere other than a cold car, although the garden already stays open until dusk anyway.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: "Although" signals contrast where there is none and leaves out the point about hours.

options.text: Because the garden already stays open until dusk, a picnic table and outlet under the awning would let students work somewhere besides a cold car at all hours.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Wrongly makes the hours the reason for the table, and "at all hours" contradicts closing at dusk.

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the statement "Nobody who gave did anything wrong; they did, in fact, something lovely" most directly addresses the audience's

options.text: likely fear that a critique of the fundraising page is also an accusation against the people who donated to it
options.label: correct
options.why: The audience includes donors (paragraph 6 addresses 'you who gave'); before the writer attacks the system, this sentence reassures donors that they are not the target, keeping them receptive to the rebuttal that follows in 'But a lifeboat is not a harbor.'

options.text: expectation that the column will ask them to give again, this time to the page built for Aurelio Dansk
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never asks readers to donate to Aurelio's page or to anyone; paragraph 6 asks only that they remember, and the passage's demand is structural, not for a second collection.

options.text: suspicion that the writer, as a friend of Lenore, is too close to the story to judge the campaign fairly
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence is about the donors' conduct, not the writer's credibility; the writer's closeness to Lenore is handled elsewhere (paragraph 6) and this sentence makes no claim about his own objectivity.

options.text: assumption that the critique in paragraph 3 was mistaken and that Lenore's page was simply more deserving
options.label: reversal
options.why: Far from retracting paragraph 3, the writer immediately pivots with 'But' to the lifeboat metaphor and the claim about outsourced stinginess; the praise of donors sets up the critique rather than withdrawing it.

items.stem: The writer's phrasing "you who gave twenty dollars or two hundred" in paragraph 6 most likely serves to

options.text: include every donor in the final request regardless of amount, treating the readers as ordinary neighbors rather than wealthy benefactors
options.label: correct
options.why: The range of modest sums names the typical reader as a small-scale giver and makes the address inclusive, so the instruction to 'Remember' and 'Remember also' lands on the whole community of donors the column is aimed at.

options.text: suggest that the smaller contributions mattered less to the final total than the larger ones listed on the page
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nothing ranks donors by size; the pairing puts twenty and two hundred on equal footing, and the passage elsewhere treats the collective giving as the point, not individual sums.

options.text: rebuke readers whose gifts were too small to cover the dialysis costs and the lost rent described in paragraph 2
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The tone of paragraph 6 is tender and grateful ('Remember the mittens'); the writer's complaint is that readers were asked at all, not that they gave too little.

options.text: demonstrate that the writer tracked each donation closely enough to know what individual readers had contributed
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The two figures are illustrative round amounts, not a record; the passage gives no indication the writer reviewed individual donations, and the phrase works as a general address, not as evidence of research.

items.stem: The niece's report in paragraph 4 that on the worst mornings the page "was the first thing she opened, before the pill organizer, before the coffee" is used chiefly to support the writer's acknowledgment that

options.text: the comfort the page gave Lenore was as real as the money it raised
options.label: correct
options.why: The detail directly follows the concession 'the money was real, and so was the comfort' and illustrates that comfort concretely, showing the page's emotional value before the writer turns to his rebuttal.

options.text: the campaign covered dialysis costs, clinic travel, and three months of lost rent
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Those financial results are established in paragraph 2 with the timeline of goals; the morning ritual is about emotional sustenance, not what the money paid for.

options.text: a system that makes the sick audition for survival has outsourced its stinginess
options.label: partially_right
options.why: That claim is the writer's rebuttal later in the same paragraph; the niece's detail belongs to the concession the writer grants before 'But,' and it does not demonstrate stinginess.

options.text: Lenore would have disliked being made an example of in a public column
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Her reluctance about publicity appears in paragraphs 2 and 6, but the detail here shows her eagerly reading the page, which if anything cuts the other way; it is not offered for that claim.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the sentence "It worked for her, for a while, because she was a story that was easy to tell, and even that was not enough in the end" qualifies the preceding claim "It does not work" primarily by

options.text: admitting a temporary exception while attributing it to Lenore's appeal as a story rather than to the arrangement itself, so the denial is honest but still stands
options.label: correct
options.why: The qualification concedes 'for her, for a while,' but the reason given, that she was 'easy to tell,' isolates popularity as the cause, and 'not enough in the end' closes the exception, so the indictment survives intact.

options.text: withdrawing the denial by granting that the arrangement does function reliably for people who are widely known in their communities
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence does not say the system works for the well known; it says it worked 'for a while' and 'even that was not enough,' which denies reliability rather than granting it.

options.text: restricting the critique to cases of kidney disease, where the clinic's distance made costs unusually hard to meet
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Nothing in the sentence limits the claim to a disease or to travel costs; the argument throughout is about who gets known and funded, not about a particular illness.

options.text: shifting responsibility onto Lenore by implying she cultivated a public image that drew donations away from others
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage shows Lenore resisting publicity ('she did not want her face on the internet'); being 'a story that was easy to tell' describes how others saw her, not anything she did.

items.stem: The final sentence of paragraph 1, "I want to honor that figure, and I want to tell the truth about it, and I am not sure the two can be done in the same breath," previews the organization of the column by

options.text: announcing two tasks that the column then takes in sequence, tribute to Lenore and the campaign first, critique of what the figure conceals afterward
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraphs 1 and 2 honor Lenore and narrate the page's success; paragraph 3 opens 'Here is the part the eulogies have skipped' and turns to truth-telling, so the sentence forecasts the two-part movement and the tension between them.

options.text: promising a chronological account of Lenore's illness from the first diagnosis through the final week before her death
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The column is organized by argument, not by medical timeline; after paragraph 2 it leaves Lenore's story to compare Aurelio's case and define charity against justice.

options.text: signaling that the writer will decline to honor the figure at all, since honesty about it makes celebration impossible
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly wants to honor the figure and does so, returning in paragraph 6 to 'the mittens, the snow, the grin'; the doubt is about doing both at once, not about refusing one.

options.text: forecasting a comparison between the two fundraising templates used by Lenore's niece and Aurelio's daughter
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: The identical template is a single detail in paragraph 3 used to rule out a variable; the sentence previews honoring versus truth-telling, a far broader frame than the pages' design.

items.stem: The placement of the sentence "Here is the part the eulogies have skipped" at the opening of paragraph 3 primarily serves to

options.text: mark the turn from tribute to critique and set the column apart from the conventional memorials it has resembled so far
options.label: correct
options.why: After two paragraphs of warm narration, this sentence announces omitted material and introduces Aurelio Dansk, shifting the tone to confrontation and distinguishing the column from the eulogies.

options.text: summarize the account of the campaign's success in paragraph 2 before the writer moves on to its financial details
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The sentence looks forward to something new ('the part... skipped'), not back; the financial details of Lenore's campaign have already been given in paragraph 2.

options.text: introduce evidence that the eulogies overstated the total raised on Lenore's fundraising page
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never disputes the 53,400 dollar figure; what the eulogies skipped is Aurelio's parallel case, not an error in Lenore's total.

options.text: dismiss the preceding praise of Lenore as sentimental and insincere in light of her neighbor's experience
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer never retracts the tribute; paragraph 6 repeats it ('Remember the mittens'), and paragraph 4 insists the donors 'did... something lovely.' The sentence adds to the story rather than discrediting it.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the structure of the sentence "Charity is what one person chooses to give; justice is what no person should have to ask for" chiefly emphasizes the relationship between the two ideas by

options.text: placing the two terms in identical clause frames so that the contrast falls on the few words that differ: who acts and whether the act is voluntary
options.label: correct
options.why: Both clauses follow the pattern 'X is what... person...,' so the differences, 'one' versus 'no' and 'chooses to give' versus 'should have to ask for,' carry the whole distinction the next sentence builds on.

options.text: subordinating the clause about justice to the clause about charity so that justice appears to follow as a consequence of giving
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are coordinate, joined by a semicolon with neither dependent on the other; the passage argues charity cannot substitute for justice, not that one produces the other.

options.text: balancing the two clauses so evenly that the terms appear interchangeable, preparing the reader to accept the blurring the writer describes
options.label: reversal
options.why: The balance sharpens the difference rather than erasing it; the following sentence treats blurring the two as the error that makes 'the Aurelios of the world invisible.'

options.text: making the second clause noticeably longer to signal that justice is the more complicated and contested of the two concepts
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The clauses are nearly equal in length and the passage never calls justice complicated; its point is that justice is simply what should not have to be requested.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the writer's reference to "a parent watching a child's enthusiasm curdle at the first hard page" most directly serves to

options.text: extend the argument to readers who are not learners themselves but who shape the conditions in which a learner meets failure
options.label: correct
options.why: The sentence pairs the prospective adult learner with a parent and asks both to notice "which kind of failure is on offer in the room," inviting the parent to apply the verdict/message distinction to a child's experience.

options.text: suggest that children abandon instruments more quickly than adults because they lack the patience to work through hard passages
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never compares children's and adults' persistence; the parent is addressed as an observer of the child's environment, not as evidence about children's patience.

options.text: remind readers that the writer's teaching experience includes young students as well as the adults described earlier
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage indicates the writer teaches children; the school's students described are adults, and the parent is addressed as a reader, not as a client.

options.text: concede that the Wednesday exercise cannot be adapted for children, whose mistakes carry less information than adults' do
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The sentence is an appeal to the reader, not a concession about the exercise; the concessions in paragraph 6 concern moves, diagnoses, and talent, not children's suitability.

items.stem: The figures in paragraph 5 concerning the twenty-six students who passed through the Wednesday group are offered primarily as evidence that

options.text: students who practice hearing mistakes as information become more skillful players than their peers within a year
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer explicitly denies this: "They do not play better than the others, at least not at first." The figures measure enrollment, not skill.

options.text: the school-wide dropout problem described in paragraph 1 has been largely resolved since the exercise was introduced
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The comparison is between the Wednesday group and a school-wide rate of "roughly half," which shows the school-wide problem persists outside the group.

options.text: a deliberate practice of naming errors is associated with students continuing their lessons rather than quitting
options.label: correct
options.why: Twenty-two of twenty-six remained enrolled against a school-wide rate of roughly half, and the paragraph concludes "They quit less," tying the figures to retention.

options.text: adult learners enjoy an exercise they find ridiculous once they understand its purpose and see its results
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph says the students find the exercise "faintly ridiculous" and name it "not entirely kindly"; the figures address retention, not enjoyment.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the statement that "a practiced ear for one's own mistakes is not the same thing as talent, whatever talent is" qualifies the writer's argument by

options.text: limiting the claim to persistence rather than ability, so that the writer is not read as promising that the exercise produces gifted players
options.label: correct
options.why: The sentence follows "I do not want to overstate what a Wednesday can do" and separates the trained ear from talent, consistent with paragraph 5's point that the Wednesday students "quit less" rather than play better.

options.text: admitting that the verdict a student hears in a wrong note may sometimes be an accurate judgment about that student's lack of talent
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage consistently rejects the verdict reading of a wrong note; the sentence distinguishes the ear from talent without endorsing the verdict.

options.text: conceding that only students who already possess talent can benefit from learning to hear mistakes as information
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never ties the benefit of the exercise to prior talent; the Wednesday group's retention results are presented without any screening for ability.

options.text: dismissing the idea of talent as meaningless so that the writer's method appears to be the only real factor in musical progress
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The aside "whatever talent is" expresses uncertainty about the term, not dismissal, and the sentence sits within a passage that is explicitly refusing to overstate the method.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between paragraph 2 and paragraph 3?

options.text: Paragraph 2 presents a case the writer regards as unusual, and paragraph 3 explains why most adult students do not respond to mistakes as Ruth did
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ruth is introduced with "Consider" as representative of the pattern in paragraph 1, and paragraph 3 describes the verdict response as the one adult learners most need to unlearn, not as rare.

options.text: Paragraph 2 describes a specific student's response to one mistake, and paragraph 3 draws from it the general distinction the rest of the passage depends on
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 3 opens "That distinction is the one I most want adult learners to understand," referring back to sentence 11's contrast between information about the hand and a sentence on the whole person, then defines it in general terms.

options.text: Paragraph 2 establishes the writer's credibility as a teacher, and paragraph 3 uses that credibility to recommend a particular exercise
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Credibility is established in paragraphs 1 and 5 (eleven years, running the Wednesday group); paragraph 3 defines a distinction and does not recommend an exercise.

options.text: Paragraph 2 raises the question of why Ruth's hearing was accurate, and paragraph 3 answers it by describing how professionals train their ears
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Paragraph 3 does mention professionals, but it does not describe training methods, and paragraph 2 is concerned with how Ruth interpreted the note, not with the accuracy of her hearing.

items.stem: The comparison in paragraph 5 of the students to "mechanics discussing a carburetor" most effectively advances the writer's purpose by

options.text: showing the group adopting the detached, diagnostic attitude toward error that paragraph 3 described as the information stance
options.label: correct
options.why: Mechanics treat a malfunction as a problem to locate and fix; the students saying "the thumb got left behind" with that calm enact hearing a wrong note as "a report about what your hand did," the information reading defined in paragraph 3.

options.text: implying that playing the cello is essentially a mechanical skill that any adult can master through sufficient repetition
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The simile describes the manner of discussing mistakes, not the nature of cello playing; the writer elsewhere declines to make claims about talent or mastery.

options.text: lending the exercise a seriousness that counters the students' sense that Wrong Note Wednesdays are faintly ridiculous
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The writer agrees the exercise is "faintly ridiculous" in the very next sentence rather than disputing it; the simile characterizes attitude toward error, not the exercise's dignity.

options.text: suggesting that the students have come to regard their instruments with the same indifference they feel toward a car engine
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: The calm belongs to the discussion of mistakes, not to the students' feelings about their instruments; the passage portrays these adults as invested enough to keep enrolling.

items.stem: In paragraph 3, the structure of the sentence "Professional musicians are not people who have stopped making mistakes; they are people who have learned to hear a wrong note as a question rather than an answer" primarily emphasizes

options.text: that professionals differ from beginners mainly in the number of wrong notes they produce during a performance
options.label: reversal
options.why: The first clause explicitly denies that professionals have stopped making mistakes; the sentence locates the difference in interpretation, not frequency.

options.text: the writer's reluctance to define what a professional musician is, since the sentence offers only what such a musician is not
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The first clause is a negation, but the second clause supplies a positive definition, so the sentence does define the professional rather than avoiding it.

options.text: a correction of a likely assumption, replacing a definition based on flawless playing with one based on how mistakes are heard
options.label: correct
options.why: The parallel clauses, "are not people who... ; they are people who...," first reject the expected standard (no mistakes) and then substitute the writer's standard (hearing a wrong note as a question), making the contrast the point.

options.text: an equal balance between two valid descriptions of expertise, inviting readers to choose the one that fits their experience
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are not offered as alternatives of equal standing; the first is negated and the second affirmed, so the structure argues rather than invites choice.

items.stem: At the end of paragraph 5, the effect of the brief sentence "They quit less" following the longer sentences about retention figures is to

options.text: state the exercise's actual benefit in deliberately plain terms, keeping the claim modest after the figures might have raised expectations
options.label: correct
options.why: After the detailed figures and the disclaimer that the students "do not play better," the three-word sentence lands the precise, limited claim with blunt emphasis, matching the writer's refusal to overstate in paragraph 6.

options.text: convey the writer's frustration that the exercise has not produced the improvement in playing that was originally hoped for
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Nothing suggests frustration; retention is exactly the problem the passage set out in paragraph 1, so the sentence registers the result the writer most wanted.

options.text: signal a shift from describing the exercise to arguing that it should be adopted by every community music school
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never proposes institutional adoption; the next paragraph instead qualifies what the exercise can do and turns to individual readers.

options.text: dismiss the students' view that the exercise is ridiculous by showing that its results speak for themselves
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The writer shares the students' view that the exercise is faintly ridiculous and does not dispute it; the short sentence summarizes the outcome rather than rebutting an opinion.

items.stem: In paragraph 6, the colon in the sentence "Some students leave for reasons no exercise can touch: a move, a diagnosis, a grandchild who needs the spare room where the cello lived" is effective primarily because it

options.text: separates the writer's own reasons for leaving teaching from the reasons the students give, clarifying whose experience is described
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer has not left teaching and gives no personal reasons; both halves of the sentence concern students.

options.text: introduces concrete particulars that make the preceding general concession credible and humane rather than merely dutiful
options.label: correct
options.why: The clause before the colon states an abstract limit on the exercise; the items after it, ending with the grandchild and the spare room, give that limit specific weight, so the concession reads as genuinely felt.

options.text: creates suspense about which of the three reasons the writer considers most responsible for the school's dropout rate
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The list is not ranked and the writer draws no conclusion about which reason dominates; the point is that none of these reasons can be addressed by the exercise.

options.text: marks the point where the paragraph turns from qualifying the argument to addressing the reader directly as a prospective learner
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: The turn to direct address occurs two sentences later with "But if you are an adult"; the colon sentence is still within the qualification.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a closing sentence after sentence 14 that eases the worry of classmates who have never done outdoor work and ends with a clear call to join the crew. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: No experience is needed, because crew leaders teach every task on the spot, so bring a friend and come help keep the trail open.
options.label: correct
options.why: It speaks directly to newcomers' lack of experience with a reassuring detail and closes with a specific invitation to volunteer.

options.text: The Tamsett Trail Association has kept the path open for many years, and its crews have rebuilt dozens of washed-out sections.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: It gives background on the association but neither calms newcomers' worries nor asks readers to come.

options.text: Experienced hikers who already know how to swing a pulaski will find the spring crew day especially rewarding this year.
options.label: reversal
options.why: It speaks to experienced volunteers, which may make students with no outdoor experience feel even more out of place.

options.text: Trail work can be dangerous and exhausting, so only students in excellent physical shape should think about signing up.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: It discourages the same newcomers the writer is trying to recruit, which works against the editorial's persuasive purpose.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it moves smoothly from building a trail (paragraph 2) to maintaining it, making clear that the work goes on after construction is finished. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Yet finishing a stretch of trail is only the beginning, because maintenance never ends.
options.label: correct
options.why: It connects the finished construction to the ongoing upkeep and shows that the work continues after building.

options.text: As a result of this slow building process, maintenance never ends.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: It wrongly says slow construction causes the endless maintenance, when winter storms are the cause.

options.text: Similarly, building a trail with pulaskis never ends either.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: It stays on building rather than moving to maintenance, so it does not make the shift the paragraph needs.

options.text: For instance, the crew near Bramble Gap had maintenance problems.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: It presents an example the draft never gives and does not state the general point that upkeep is ongoing.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 3, the last sentence of the introduction, so that it presents the puzzle her report will investigate: how a person who makes no sound can still lead the players. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Yet she is the only person on the stage who makes no sound, so I set out to learn how the players know what she wants.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the silent-player fact and turns it into the guiding question of how silent leadership works, which paragraphs 2 and 3 answer.

options.text: She is the only person on the stage who makes no sound, and she has led the orchestra for many seasons.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Adds a background fact rather than raising the question the report investigates.

options.text: Yet she makes no sound at all, which proves that conductors are the most important musicians in any orchestra.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a sweeping ranking claim the report never supports, and it doesn't raise the question of how she leads.

options.text: She makes no sound at all, and I wondered how youth orchestras around the world choose their conductors.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Raises a question about how conductors are chosen, which the report never takes up.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 5 that gives further evidence for the cellist's specific claim in sentence 4, that the musicians follow the conductor's breath more closely than her baton. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me she had been watching the conductor's rising shoulders, not the baton tip.
options.label: correct
options.why: A second player confirms she watched the breath (rising shoulders) rather than the baton, which directly supports the claim.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me the overture is one of the hardest pieces the orchestra has learned.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Says how hard the piece is, which has nothing to do with breath or the baton.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me she always keeps her eyes fixed on the tip of the conductor's baton.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Supports the baton instead of the breath, so it works against the claim.

options.text: Afterward, a violist told me that breathing exercises help wind players hold long notes more steadily.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Mentions breathing, but it's about players' own technique, not about following the conductor's breath.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a comparison after sentence 10 that advances her argument that a conductor's gestures are signals the players have learned to read. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Like a word in a shared language, the lowered hand meant softer only because the players had learned it together.
options.label: correct
options.why: The language comparison shows the gesture works through learned, shared meaning, which is the argument's main point.

options.text: Like a traffic officer at a busy corner, she stood in the center where everyone could see her.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Compares her to someone who directs others, but the point is visibility, not learned signals.

options.text: Like a painter at a blank canvas, she seemed to create the music entirely by herself.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Suggests she makes the music alone, which ignores the players reading her signals.

options.text: Like a storm rolling slowly over the valley, the sound of the brass faded into the quiet hall.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A decorative image of the sound fading that says nothing about how gestures carry meaning.

items.stem: Taken together, the details of the passage suggest that the writer is responding most directly to which of the following situations?

options.text: A published redevelopment plan that is still open to amendment for a limited period
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 1 states the Council 'has published its plan,' and paragraph 6 tells Council members they 'have until the end of the month to amend this plan,' establishing a plan under public review as the occasion.

options.text: A recent electrical accident at the market that has renewed calls for the stalls to be rewired
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer calls the wiring a hazard and mentions cords in puddles, but no accident is described; the hazard is background, not the triggering event.

options.text: The failure of the Marrow Lane market, which has prompted the city to reconsider covered pavilions
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Marrow Lane is offered by the writer as a cautionary precedent in paragraph 4; nothing suggests the city is reconsidering anything because of it.

options.text: The announced closing of the market's original stalls, which the writer hopes to delay
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The plan would replace the stalls, but it has not been finalized or scheduled; the writer seeks amendment of a proposal, not a delay of an announced closing.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the writer's stance toward the Council's plan as a whole?

options.text: Firm opposition to its reorganization of vendors, combined with acceptance of its safety goals
options.label: correct
options.why: The writer concedes the wiring and drainage must be fixed (paragraphs 3 and 6, 'None of this means the market should stay dangerous') while rejecting selection, lotteries, and higher rents.

options.text: Reluctant endorsement of the pavilion, softened by regret that the old stalls will be lost
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer does not endorse the pavilion as proposed; she asks the Council to 'leave the stalls where they are' and grant families tenure, which the plan does not do.

options.text: Open contempt for the planners, whom she treats as indifferent to the market's history
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: She says 'I want to be fair to the people who wrote it' and notes the renderings reproduce the market's details 'lovingly'; the tone is critical, not contemptuous.

options.text: Resigned acceptance that the market's customs will vanish however the plan is revised
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Paragraph 6 lays out specific amendments she believes would preserve the customs, so she is not resigned to their loss.

items.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.text: Because a market's character lies in long-held habits rather than in its appearance, the Council should repair hazards but leave the stalls and vendors in place
options.label: correct
options.why: Paragraph 5 defines character as 'a set of habits held by particular people over a long time,' and paragraph 6 draws the practical conclusion: fix wiring and drains, then leave stalls and tenure intact.

options.text: Because the market grew without planning and thrived for sixty years, the city should continue to leave it entirely alone
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The writer explicitly rejects leaving the market as it is: 'None of this means the market should stay dangerous,' and she asks for wiring and drains to be fixed.

options.text: Because the Council's renderings preserve the lanterns, sailcloth, and handwritten signs, the plan protects what matters most about the market
options.label: reversal
options.why: The writer argues the opposite: the renderings capture a look, and 'character, in a market, is not a look.'

options.text: Because the Marrow Lane pavilion lost a third of its vendors within a year, covered markets of this kind cannot succeed anywhere
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Marrow Lane is supporting evidence for one approach, not a universal claim; the writer even allows that the Council 'can give Halvern Street a roof.'

items.stem: In paragraph 4, the detail that the committee filled vacancies with "a coffee franchise and a shop selling scented candles" is used primarily to support the claim that

options.text: a selection process ends up installing a generic commercial mix in place of the vendors it set out to keep
options.label: correct
options.why: The detail shows what a 'selection committee' does once chosen vendors leave, illustrating the writer's objection to a 'curated vendor mix' in paragraph 3 and the untransferable habits in paragraph 5.

options.text: rents set above informal levels drive out established vendors within a single season
options.label: partially_right
options.why: The departure of a third of vendors supports that point; the franchise and candle shop concern who replaces them, not why they left.

options.text: an ordinance requiring a nine o'clock closing makes a night market unprofitable
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The closing hour is a separate detail used for the juxtaposition with Halvern Street's hours, not what the replacement shops demonstrate.

options.text: a covered steel roof and uniform counters make a market physically less safe than open stalls
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The writer never claims the Marrow Lane structure was unsafe; she concedes safety is the one thing the Council's plan gets right.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the function of paragraph 5 within the passage as a whole?

options.text: It redefines the key term so that the Marrow Lane failure is explained and the proposal that follows is justified
options.label: correct
options.why: By defining character as habits that 'took sixty years' and 'are not transferable to whoever wins a lottery,' paragraph 5 accounts for why Marrow Lane emptied and grounds the paragraph 6 request to keep families in place.

options.text: It concedes that the Council's renderings capture the market accurately before turning to the question of cost
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The paragraph grants only that the renderings reproduce a look, and it does not turn to cost; rents were raised in paragraph 3.

options.text: It returns to the writer's childhood memories to restore the warm tone of the opening paragraph
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The paragraph is analytical, not reminiscent; the examples (Orano's grandson, the spilled bucket) are generalized customs, not the writer's memories.

options.text: It introduces a new objection to the plan unrelated to the vendor selection discussed in earlier paragraphs
options.label: reversal
options.why: The paragraph deepens the existing objection to selection and lotteries rather than adding a separate one; its closing clause names the lottery directly.

items.stem: In paragraph 5, the writer's observation that the Council's renderings reproduce the market's details "so lovingly" primarily serves to

options.text: suggest that the Council's careful attention is sincere but aimed at the wrong thing
options.label: correct
options.why: The word credits the planners with real care, which makes the immediate rebuttal ('But character, in a market, is not a look') land as a correction of focus rather than an accusation of bad faith.

options.text: mock the planners for sentimentality that the writer herself refuses to indulge
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: The writer opened with her own affectionate memory of lanterns; she is not positioning herself against sentiment, and the word is wry, not mocking.

options.text: praise the renderings as evidence that the plan will preserve the market's character
options.label: reversal
options.why: The next sentences deny that the look is character at all, so the word cannot be endorsing the renderings as preservation.

options.text: show that the writer admires the Council's design more than the current stalls
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Nothing in the passage expresses preference for the designed pavilion; she asks that the stalls be left where they are.

items.stem: In the sentence "A pavilion can be built in eighteen months; the habits took sixty years, and they are not transferable to whoever wins a lottery" in paragraph 5, the semicolon is effective primarily because it

options.text: sets the two time spans side by side without a connecting word, so the disparity makes the point on its own
options.label: correct
options.why: The semicolon joins two independent clauses about eighteen months and sixty years with no 'but' or 'while,' letting the bare contrast in scale carry the argument before the added clause draws the conclusion.

options.text: signals that the second clause is a consequence of the first, showing how construction destroys the habits
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The clauses are contrasted, not causally linked; the pavilion's construction time does not produce the sixty-year history.

options.text: introduces a list of the specific habits the writer has just described in the preceding sentences
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A colon, not a semicolon, introduces the list of habits earlier in the paragraph; here the semicolon separates two complete statements.

options.text: softens the contrast by subordinating the second clause to the first, keeping the tone measured
options.label: reversal
options.why: The semicolon coordinates equal clauses rather than subordinating, and the effect sharpens rather than softens the contrast.

items.stem: The opening sentence of the passage places the clause "On the night in 1987 when the power failed along Halvern Street" before the main clause "my aunt Ines kept frying." This arrangement primarily emphasizes

options.text: the aunt's steady continuation of her work despite the disruption
options.label: correct
options.why: Leading with the blackout sets up an expectation of interruption, so the short main clause 'kept frying' lands as the emphasized idea: ordinary persistence in the face of failure.

options.text: the seriousness of the electrical hazards the writer later concedes
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: The blackout here is a setting for the lantern anecdote, not evidence of hazard; the wiring concession comes in paragraph 3 with separate details.

options.text: the precise historical moment when the market began to decline
options.label: unsupported
options.why: The passage never describes a decline beginning in 1987; the market 'accumulated' and the city 'left it alone' for sixty years.

options.text: the writer's distance from events she knows only through family stories
options.label: reversal
options.why: The sentence and paragraph present the writer as a witness ('I think of those lanterns now'), not as someone relying on secondhand accounts.
